meta.description: Anne Rice, not Kafka. She wrote it on page 3 of her foreword to a 1995 Schocken collection of Kafka's stories — describing him, not quoting him.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Don't Bend; Don't Water It Down; Don't Try to Make It Logical; Don't Edit Your Own Soul According to the Fashion'?
meta.ogDescription: Anne Rice wrote it in her 1995 foreword to a Kafka collection. The internet has spent years crediting it to Kafka. Rice confirmed it was hers in 2015.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Anne Rice wrote these words in her foreword to a 1995 Schocken Books collection of Franz Kafka’s stories — describing what Kafka’s example taught her, not quoting him. Quote Investigator located the passage on page 3 of that foreword from library scans, and Rice herself confirmed authorship in 2015.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: The Metamorphosis, In the Penal Colony, and Other Stories

Kafka’s stories translated by Willa and Edwin Muir — but this sentence is Rice’s own English, not a translation

source.excerpt: Kafka became a model for me, a continuing inspiration. … Don’t bend; don’t water it down; don’t try to make it logical; don’t edit your own soul according to the fashion. Rather, follow your most intense obsessions mercilessly.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ traced the passage to page 3 of Anne Rice’s foreword and reports the 1995 citation was “verified with scans” obtained through the Beaufort County Library system of South Carolina.
Penguin Random House’s own catalogue record for ISBN 9780805210576 ↗ lists the Schocken edition as “Foreword by Anne Rice” and “Translated by Willa and Edwin Muir”, published 14 November 1995.
Wikiquote ↗ files the line in Kafka’s “Misattributed” section, noting it is confirmed to be from Anne Rice.
The error is still live: the Goodreads quote page ↗ continues to credit Franz Kafka, with no source named.
source.excerptNote: Rice used no quotation marks anywhere in this passage, because she was not quoting Kafka — she was describing what his work seemed to be telling her to do. That absence of quotation marks is precisely what let the sentence travel as if it were his.

source.rightsNote: This sentence comes from Anne Rice’s foreword, first published by Schocken Books in 1995 — comfortably inside copyright in the United States. Kafka’s own German texts are long in the public domain and the Muir translations are of their own era, but none of that touches Rice’s foreword, which is a separate 1995 work by an identifiable author. Quoted here briefly for identification and comment.

author.name: Anne Rice
author.heading: Who was Anne Rice?
author.bio: Anne Rice (born Howard Allen Frances O’Brien in New Orleans, 4 October 1941; died 11 December 2021) was an American author of Gothic fiction, erotic literature and Bible fiction, best known for Interview with the Vampire and the rest of The Vampire Chronicles. She wrote occasional forewords and introductions to other writers’ books, including a 1995 Schocken Books edition of Kafka’s stories. It is that foreword — not any novel — that produced the sentence the internet spent years crediting to Kafka.

misattribution.heading: Credited to Kafka almost everywhere
misattribution.intro: This is a misattribution that runs backwards from the usual pattern: the quotation is genuine and the author is real, but the name attached to it online is almost always the wrong one. Because Anne Rice wrote the sentence inside a book of Franz Kafka’s stories, Kafka got the credit.

items.why: Rice was paraphrasing what Kafka’s example seemed to tell her, and used no quotation marks because she was not quoting him. Quote Investigator reports that it located no substantive evidence that Kafka said or wrote the passage ↗.

items.who: Russell Brand, Booky Wook 2: This Time It’s Personal (HarperCollins, 2010)
items.why: Quote Investigator records the line as the epigraph on the first page of the 2010 sequel, attributed there to Franz Kafka ↗ — the enquiry that prompted the investigation in the first place.
Quote Investigator dates a Kafka credit on Goodreads to 2009; the page still reads “― Franz Kafka” ↗, with no book or page given. Goodreads notes that community quotes are not verified.

misattribution.truthLine: Rice settled it herself. In a Facebook message dated 26 June 2015, quoted in full by Quote Investigator ↗, she wrote that a remark from her introduction to a Kafka collection was “being attributed worldwide to Kafka” — and that they were her own words.

context.heading: Why this one travelled
lead: The sentence is a novelist’s attempt to say what another novelist taught her — and because Anne Rice wrote it without quotation marks, inside a book with Franz Kafka’s name on the cover, it escaped into the world wearing his name instead of hers. It reads like Kafka giving advice. It is actually Rice explaining what she heard Kafka saying.

When Quote Investigator reached her in June 2015, Rice found the whole thing funny rather than annoying. Her own account is the cleanest summary anyone has managed: she had written a short introduction to a Kafka collection, and a line about Kafka’s influence on her had come back to her from all over the internet as a line by Kafka.
context.detailsSummary: How a foreword turned into a Kafka quotation
detailsBody: A foreword is a structurally dangerous place to write a memorable sentence. The paraphrase sits a few pages from the author’s own text, in the author’s own book, and once it is lifted out of the page nothing in the words themselves says which of the two writers is speaking.

Quote Investigator’s chronology shows how far it got before anyone checked: a Goodreads entry credited it to Kafka in 2009, and by 2010 it stood as the epigraph on the first page of Russell Brand’s memoir Booky Wook 2, credited to Kafka there too. A Kafka birthday post on an Anne Rice fan page in July 2013 — crediting Kafka — is the neatest illustration of how thoroughly the real author had been written out.
context.pull: Those are my words struggling to define the impression Kafka’s example made on me!

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator concludes the quotation should be credited to Anne Rice, not Franz Kafka; she wrote it in the foreword to a 1995 Schocken Books collection of Kafka's stories, on page 3, foreword dated June 1995, verified with scans via the Beaufort County Library. QI also documents the Russell Brand 'Booky Wook 2' (2010, HarperCollins) epigraph crediting Kafka, a 2009 Goodreads Kafka credit, a July 2013 Anne Rice fan page post crediting Kafka, and Rice's 26 June 2015 Facebook message confirming the words are hers.

Wikiquote's Franz Kafka page lists 'Don't bend; don't water it down; don't try to make it logical; don't edit your own soul according to the fashion. Rather, follow your most intense obsessions mercilessly.' under the heading 'Misattributed', noting it is confirmed to be from Anne Rice.
Penguin Random House's catalogue record for ISBN 9780805210576 lists the Schocken title with 'Foreword by Anne Rice' and 'Translated by Willa and Edwin Muir', publication date 14 November 1995.
The Internet Archive holds a scan catalogued as 'The metamorphosis, In the penal colony, and other stories' by Franz Kafka, publisher Schocken Books, date 1995, ISBN 0805210571 / 9780805210576.
The Goodreads quote page for this line attributes it to Franz Kafka ('― Franz Kafka') with no source book named, and states that community-added quotes are not verified by Goodreads.

Anne Rice was born Howard Allen Frances O'Brien on 4 October 1941 in New Orleans and died 11 December 2021; she was an American author of Gothic fiction, erotic literature and Bible fiction, best known for The Vampire Chronicles.

AbeBooks lists ISBN 9780805210576 as 'Metamorphosis, in the Penal Colony, and Other Stories (Schocken Kafka Library) - Franz Kafka; Anne Rice (Foreword)', Schocken Books, 1995, with the synopsis line 'New Foreword by Anne Rice.'
